## Critique
- claim-1: Correctly grounded. Specializing \(n=10,r=s=5,t=4\) gives \(i=j=2\), \(a=3\), \(b=2\), and the cited theorem supplies generation of the lower-adjoined family.
- claim-2: Correctly grounded by the cited remark. Moreover, right-family generation follows independently by applying the ideal-preserving automorphism \(\omega\) to the lower generating family.
- claim-3: Supported as accepted, exact finite computation by the two cited artifacts, not as an external source-backed fact. The complementary minors certify the ten lower classes in degrees \(4,\dots,10\), while the all-support computation excludes further quotient classes.
- claim-4: The proof is complete. Since \(5^5\) and \(22\) are self-conjugate, \(\omega(I_{5,5})=I_{5,5}\) and \(\omega(J)=J\). Homogeneity gives \(\omega(A_+)=A_+\), hence \(\omega(A_+J)=A_+J\), so \(\omega\) induces an involution of \(Q\). The displayed conjugates are correct and exhaust the right-adjoined interval \(22\subseteq\mu\subseteq5^2\).
- claim-5: The accepted indexed-family Nakayama criterion applies: each ten-element family generates \(J\) and maps to a \(\mathbb Z\)-basis of \(Q\), so each is irredundant. The strategy reaches the requested case-specific two-family minimality conclusion.

## Required revisions
- None for the explicitly stated specialization \((i,j,p,c)=(2,2,3,3)\). The argument must not be presented as proving arbitrary \(i,j\) with \(p=c=3\).
